title: The Ravidassia community
hook: a community who revere Guru Ravidas and now keep their own scripture

segments.voice: Yesterday, beyond caste names: Singh and Kaur, one shared name so nobody could read your birth off it. Your line was one name for all. Who did you ask something new, before asking where they were from? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-four.

A hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib carries the name Ravidas, the poet tradition remembers as a shoemaker of Benares. In a gurdwara, it's sung as one voice among many in a great book. Across town, under a different symbol, the same words are sung as the voice of the one the room calls Guru. Same poet, same words. A different center. Year three met the community who keep Ravidas at that center. Today we go back to them, because something has changed in how they keep him.
screen: `ONE VOICE AMONG MANY.` → `THE SAME WORDS, ANOTHER ROOM.` → `A DIFFERENT CENTER.`

segments.voice: First, who they are. The Ravidassia community revere Guru Ravidas as their Guru. The community includes families from the same communities Ravidas himself came from, the ones the old order counted low. For them, a shoemaker who sang his way past every wall of caste is not one voice among many. He is the voice. Second, what has changed. For a long time, the Guru Granth Sahib was installed in Ravidassia places of worship, just as in a gurdwara. In recent years, the Ravidassia community has gathered Guru Ravidas's own hymns into a scripture of their own, and now install it at the center of their worship. They have their own greeting and their own symbol too. That's today's line: their own path. Third, a hymn to hold it all. In the Granth, in Raag Sorath, Ravidas sings a chain of pictures to God, here in paraphrase. You are the sandalwood, I am the water. You are the cloud, I am the peacock. You are the lamp, I am the wick. You are the master, I am the servant. Notice what each pair does. The lesser thing is never thrown away. Water takes the scent of sandalwood. The wick is what lets the lamp burn. A low thing, held close to God, becomes part of the light. Fourth, how to stand toward this. Sikhs keep singing Ravidas in the Granth with full honor. The Ravidassia community keep him at the center of a path that is now their own. Some on both sides feel the parting deeply; others call it simply a community finding its own name. Neither story needs ranking here. The same hymns are still sung in both houses.
screen: `RAVIDAS AT THE CENTER.` · `A SCRIPTURE OF THEIR OWN.` · `THE LAMP AND THE WICK.` · `SUNG IN BOTH HOUSES.` · then, large: `THEIR OWN PATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect their path. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a family or community that once shared a home with yours, a congregation, a club, a group of friends, and then went its own way. Notice anything that still stings, and let it be there. Then picture them at their own table, singing their own song, and wish them well there. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
The Ravidassia community. Those who revere Guru Ravidas as their Guru and now keep a scripture of his hymns at the center of their worship. Today's word.
Your line: their own path. Today, when someone describes their faith or their group in their own words, use their words back to them, not yours. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-four.

notes: Sensitive: the Sikh–Ravidassia relationship. Written to describe both respectfully and settle nothing. A Keeper and ideally a Ravidassia reader should check every sentence, especially 'their Guru', 'a scripture of their own' (the Amritbani, not named in the voice), 'their own greeting and their own symbol' (Jai Gurudev; the Har symbol), and 'some on both sides feel the parting deeply'.
No date is given for the new scripture ('in recent years'); please confirm that framing.
'The community includes families from the communities Ravidas himself came from' and 'now install it at the center of their worship' are stated without a cited source; please confirm.

Ang 658–659 Sorath ('prabh jee tum chandan ham paanee... tum ghan ban ham mor... tum deepak ham baatee... tum suaamee ham daasaa') paraphrased; please confirm Ang and the pairs used (moon/chakor and pearl/thread left out).
Year three (day 779) already introduced the community; today's new angle is the separate scripture. Day 1111 used Ravidas's Kedara hymn; Begampura (Ang 345) deliberately not reused.
Original ਰਵਿਦਾਸ: please confirm spelling as used in the Granth.
